name: Rinchenpong
tagline: A ridge village with a 1730 monastery and a full Kangchenjunga view
meta_description: Rinchenpong, Soreng district: 1730 monastery with a rare Ati Buddha, the Poison Lake story, homestays from ₹1,200, honest costs and how to get there.
summary: Rinchenpong is a quiet ridge village at about 1,650 m in Soreng district, 120 km from Gangtok, with one of the widest Kangchenjunga views in Sikkim. Come for the 1730 monastery and its rare Ati Buddha, the Poison Lake story, village walks and homestays from about ₹1,200 a night with meals.
intro: Rinchenpong sits on a ridge above the Rangeet valley in Soreng district, which was West Sikkim until December 2021. The bazaar is a few shops, a taxi stand and a school; the houses spread along the road towards Kaluk and up the slope to the monastery. On a clear morning from October to April the whole Kangchenjunga range fills the north-west horizon, and that view, rather than any single sight, is why people come and stay two nights instead of one.

The village's history is unusually rich for its size. Rinchenpong Monastery, founded around 1730, is described by the Soreng district administration as the third oldest in Sikkim and keeps a rare Ati Buddha (Adi Buddha) image. Below the monastery path lies Bikh Pokhari, the Poison Lake, linked locally to resistance against a British force. Reesum Gumpa crowns the hill above, and the Rabindra Smriti Van park carries the name of Rabindranath Tagore.

It is a slow place. There is no shopping street, no nightlife and no hotel larger than a village resort. Days are for walking between monasteries, farms and viewpoints, eating long meals at a homestay and watching the light on the range at dawn and dusk. Pelling is about 31 km away by road, Jorethang 32 km, and Barsey's trailhead at Hilley is a half-day drive via Soreng, so Rinchenpong pairs well with both.

story.title: The Ati Buddha of Rinchenpong Monastery
story.text: Rinchenpong Monastery was founded in about 1730 by Ngadakpa Lama, and is counted by the Soreng district administration as the third oldest monastery in Sikkim. Its Wikipedia article records that it began with around 98 lamas. What sets it apart is a rare image of the Ati Buddha, the Adi Buddha or primordial Buddha, seated in the yab-yum posture. In Vajrayana Buddhism, yab-yum (father-mother) shows a male figure in union with his female consort. It is not an image of desire: it stands for the union of compassion and wisdom, method and insight, which Vajrayana teaches must come together for enlightenment. The Ati Buddha is usually shown as a deep blue, unclothed figure, blue being the colour of the boundless sky and of the mind's original nature. Images of this kind are uncommon in Sikkim's monasteries, which makes the small hilltop gompa worth the climb. Visitors should ask the caretaker monk before entering the lhakhang, walk clockwise, and not photograph the image without permission.
story.source: Soreng district administration, soreng.nic.in (Rinchenpong Monastery); Wikipedia: Rinchenpong Monastery; Wikipedia: Yab-Yum

little_known.fact: Wikipedia's Rinchenpong article records a local account that Lepcha and Gorkha defenders poisoned the only lake on the approach with herbs, halting a British force. The site, Bikh Pokhari, is still pointed out on the monastery path.

The Rabindra Smriti Van park is named after Rabindranath Tagore. As told locally, the poet once stayed in Rinchenpong; we have not found a written record of the visit, so treat it as village tradition.
little_known.source: soreng.nic.in (Rabindranath Tagore Park); as told locally

little_known.fact: Rinchenpong Monastery is thought to have started with around 98 lamas when it was founded about 1730, a large community for a hilltop gompa in western Sikkim at the time.

facts: Kangchenjunga views, 1730 monastery, Ati Buddha image, Poison Lake, homestays
Not needed for Indians; foreigners need Sikkim's RAP (e-FRRO)

highlights.title: Rinchenpong Monastery and the Ati Buddha
highlights.text: A short steep walk or drive above the bazaar brings you to the monastery founded around 1730, the third oldest in Sikkim according to the district administration. Inside is the rare Ati Buddha in yab-yum. Go early, ask the caretaker monk before entering and leave a small offering.

highlights.title: Kangchenjunga from the ridge
highlights.text: From the upper road and the monastery yard the range runs from Kabru to Pandim across the horizon, with Kangchenjunga at 8,586 m in the middle. Sunrise from October to April is the time; by 9 am cloud often builds. Bring a warm layer, as mornings are 3–8 °C in winter.

highlights.title: Bikh Pokhari, the Poison Lake
highlights.text: A small pond near the monastery path is the Poison Lake of local memory, tied to an account of defenders poisoning the water to stop a British force. Wikipedia records the story; locals still call the water unsafe. Look, listen to the story, and do not drink or touch it.

highlights.title: Reesum Gumpa on the hilltop
highlights.text: Above Rinchenpong, in Upper Hathidhunga, Reesum Gumpa is a small wooden-and-stone monastery that the district site lists among the oldest in Sikkim. The forest walk up takes about an hour and ends at one of the best panoramic points in the area.

highlights.title: Rabindra Smriti Van
highlights.text: A small park and viewpoint named after Rabindranath Tagore, close to the Meghi Dara area. It is a pleasant evening stroll with benches facing the range. The connection to the poet is a local tradition rather than a documented visit, which we think is worth saying plainly.

highlights.title: Farm and village walks
highlights.text: Paths link Rinchenpong with Kaluk, the farms below and the heritage farmhouse at Yangsum. You walk past maize, millet, cardamom under shade trees and household orange trees, with dogs and children for company. A local guide costs about ₹800–1,500 for a half day.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps run from Jorethang to Rinchenpong and Kaluk through the day, about 1.5 hours for roughly ₹120–180 a seat. From Siliguri, take a shared jeep to Jorethang (about 3.5–4 hours, ₹250–350) and change. Morning departures are most reliable; the last jeeps up leave mid-afternoon.

A reserved small car from Pelling takes about 1.5–2 hours over roughly 31 km via Gyalshing and Legship, for about ₹2,000–2,500 one way. From Gangtok it is about 120 km and 5 hours via Singtam, Melli and Jorethang, or via Namchi, at about ₹5,000–6,500 one way.

Bagdogra airport and NJP station are about 115–125 km away, 4.5–5 hours by car via Sevoke, Melli and Jorethang, for about ₹4,500–6,000 for a small car. The Teesta road along NH10 closes after monsoon slides; drivers then go via Kalimpong. Check current status before you travel.

costs: Free; a small offering is welcome
where_to_stay: Most travellers stay in family homestays along the upper road and the monastery paths, which cost about ₹1,200–2,200 per person with meals and often face the range. For more comfort, Ghonday Village Resort and Mandarin Village Resort are a few minutes away in Kaluk, at about ₹3,000–5,500 a room. Yangsum Heritage Farm, a family farmhouse from 1833 about 2 km from the bazaar, is the characterful splurge at roughly ₹6,000–9,500 a room with meals. There are no large hotels, so book October–November and April early.
tips: Set an alarm for sunrise: from October to April the range is clearest between about 5:30 and 8 am.
Carry cash, since there is no reliable ATM in Rinchenpong; the nearest are in Soreng and Jorethang.
Ask before photographing inside Rinchenpong Monastery, and walk clockwise around the shrine.
Pack a windproof layer: the ridge between Rinchenpong and Kaluk is breezy, especially from November to February.
Combine Rinchenpong with Pelling, 31 km away, rather than doing it as a long day trip from Gangtok.

experiences.title: See the Ati Buddha at Rinchenpong Monastery
experiences.summary: Walk up to the monastery founded around 1730, counted as the third oldest in Sikkim, and see its rare Ati Buddha in yab-yum. We explain what the image means, how to behave inside, and time the visit for the morning view of Kangchenjunga.
body: The walk from Rinchenpong bazaar to the monastery is short but steep, 20–30 minutes on foot or a few minutes by car. The gompa sits at about 1,700 m among old trees, with prayer flags strung towards the ridge. It was founded around 1730 by Ngadakpa Lama, and the Soreng district administration describes it as the third oldest monastery in Sikkim. Wikipedia notes it began with about 98 lamas. Today it is quiet, with a caretaker monk and a few novices, and morning prayers when the community is present.

The reason to come is the Ati Buddha, the primordial Buddha, shown seated in yab-yum, in union with his consort. In Vajrayana Buddhism this stands for the joining of compassion and wisdom, not for desire. The figure is deep blue, the colour of open sky and of the mind's own nature. Such images are rare in Sikkim, and the monks treat it with care. Ask before entering the lhakhang, remove shoes, walk clockwise and do not photograph the image unless you are clearly told you may.

Go early. From October to April the monastery yard looks straight at the Kangchenjunga range, and by mid-morning cloud often rises from the valleys. A visit takes about 1.5 hours including the walk, and pairs well with the Poison Lake on the path below and the climb to Reesum Gumpa. Leave a small offering of ₹20–100 in the box if you wish; there is no entry fee.

faqs.q: What is the Ati Buddha at Rinchenpong Monastery?
faqs.a: It is an image of the Adi Buddha, the primordial Buddha of Vajrayana Buddhism, shown deep blue and seated in yab-yum with a female consort. The pairing symbolises the union of compassion and wisdom. The Soreng district administration calls it a very rare statue, and it is the main reason travellers make the climb to this monastery.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Rinchenpong Monastery?
faqs.a: Usually not of the main images without permission. Ask the caretaker monk first, and accept a no politely. Photographs of the exterior, the yard and the mountain view are fine. Avoid flash, do not point at images, and keep voices low if prayers are going on.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to Rinchenpong Monastery?
faqs.a: About 20–30 minutes uphill from the bazaar on a steep lane, or a few minutes by car. The path is uneven in places, so wear shoes with grip. Older travellers can drive up and walk only the last short stretch to the gompa.

experiences.title: Walk to Bikh Pokhari, the Poison Lake
experiences.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, year-round except heavy rain
experiences.summary: A short walk to the small pond that Rinchenpong remembers as the Poison Lake, where, as told locally and recorded on Wikipedia, defenders poisoned the water to stop a British force. Hear the story from a local guide and see how memory shapes a landscape.
body: Bikh Pokhari means poison pond in Nepali. It lies near the junction on the path towards Rinchenpong Monastery, a small, still body of water among trees. It is not a scenic lake, and that is not the point. The village remembers it as the place where, during a British advance into this part of Sikkim, local Lepcha and Gorkha defenders poisoned the only water source with a mix of herbs. Wikipedia's Rinchenpong article records the account, including the claim that the poisoning killed many soldiers and forced a peace.

We tell this as local tradition. We have not found a dated British record that names the place, and the details shift depending on who tells it. What is certain is that the story matters here: the pond is pointed out to every visitor, and people still say the water is unsafe. Respect that. Do not drink, wade in or throw anything into it, and keep children and dogs back from the edge.

The walk takes about an hour from the bazaar there and back, and is easiest combined with the monastery visit, since the path is the same. A local guide, about ₹500–800, adds the version of the story his own family tells, and points out medicinal plants along the way. Wear shoes with grip; after rain the path is muddy and leeches appear from June to September.

faqs.q: Is the Poison Lake in Rinchenpong really poisonous?
faqs.a: Local people say the water is still unsafe, and Wikipedia repeats the claim that it remains poisoned. We have no test results either way. Treat it as unsafe: do not drink, touch or wade in the water, and keep children and pets away from the edge.

faqs.q: Is the Poison Lake story historically proven?
faqs.a: Not as far as we can find. Wikipedia records a local account of Lepcha and Gorkha defenders poisoning the lake to halt a British force, but we have not found a British record naming the place. We tell it as village tradition, which is how most people in Rinchenpong tell it too.

faqs.q: Where exactly is Bikh Pokhari?
faqs.a: It is beside the path that climbs from Rinchenpong bazaar towards the monastery, near a junction on the left as you go up. Ask at your homestay or at the taxi stand; everyone knows it. Most visitors see it on the way to or from the monastery.

experiences.title: Kangchenjunga sunrise and Rabindra Smriti Van
experiences.summary: Watch first light turn Kangchenjunga pink from the Rinchenpong ridge, then walk to the Rabindra Smriti Van park named after Rabindranath Tagore. A simple, free morning that is the best thing to do in Rinchenpong when the sky is clear.
body: From October to April, on most clear mornings, the Kangchenjunga range stretches across the north-west horizon from Rinchenpong. Kangchenjunga itself, at 8,586 m, sits in the middle, with Kabru to the left and Pandim to the right as seen from here. The first light hits the summit about 15–20 minutes before sunrise in the village, turning it pink and then gold. Watch from your homestay balcony, the upper road or the monastery yard. Take a warm jacket, as winter mornings are 3–8 °C.

After breakfast, walk or drive to the Rabindra Smriti Van, a small park and viewpoint near Meghi Dara. The Soreng district administration lists it as a recreational spot named after Rabindranath Tagore. As told locally, the poet once stayed in Rinchenpong; we have not found a written record of the visit, so we present it as village tradition. The park has benches, flowering trees and a clear view across the valley, and it is quiet on weekday mornings.

This is a free outing that needs only an alarm clock and some luck with weather. Check the sky the night before: a clear evening with a cold breeze usually means a good dawn. From June to September cloud hides the range for days at a time, so do not plan a monsoon trip around it. Photographers should bring a telephoto lens; the summit is far away.

faqs.q: What time is sunrise in Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: Roughly 5:00–5:15 am in May and June and about 6:15–6:30 am in December and January. The summit catches light 15–20 minutes before the village does, so be outside early. October to April gives the clearest mornings; from June to September cloud usually covers the range.

faqs.q: Did Rabindranath Tagore visit Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: As told locally, yes, and the Rabindra Smriti Van park is named after him. We have not found a written record of the visit in Tagore's letters or biographies, so we present it as village tradition. The park is worth a stroll for its view whatever the history.

faqs.q: Which peaks can I see from Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: On a clear day the Kangchenjunga range spans the north-west, with Kangchenjunga (8,586 m) in the centre, Kabru to the left and Pandim to the right as seen from here. Your homestay host can name the smaller peaks. Binoculars help.

experiences.title: Farm walk from Rinchenpong to Yangsum
experiences.summary: A guided half-day on foot through the farms below Rinchenpong to Yangsum, a family farmhouse built in 1833. See how maize, millet, cardamom and oranges are grown on these slopes, and why Soreng's farmers mix crops rather than plant just one.
body: Below Rinchenpong the slope drops in terraces of maize, millet and paddy, broken by stands of alder that shade large cardamom. The walk follows village paths rather than the road, past houses with orange trees, cowsheds and drying racks. Soreng district is known for oranges, ginger, large cardamom, vegetables and flowers, and a guide from the village explains what each terrace grows in which month. Sikkim has farmed organically by state policy since it was declared India's first fully organic state in 2016.

The destination is Yangsum Heritage Farm, about 2 km from the bazaar, where a family farmhouse built in 1833 and remodelled in 1966 sits on a 44-acre organic farm. If you are not staying there, ask your guide or us to arrange a visit in advance; it is a private home, not a museum. Even from the path you see how a large farm here works, with fields, forest and water channels side by side.

Allow about three hours at an easy pace, including stops. The return is uphill, so older travellers may want a car to collect them. Wear shoes with grip and carry water. From June to September the paths are muddy and leeches are common; October to May is better. A guide costs about ₹800–1,500 for a small group.

faqs.q: Can we visit Yangsum Heritage Farm without staying there?
faqs.a: Only by arrangement. It is a private family farm and homestay, so ask in advance, either directly or through us, whether a short visit or a meal is possible on your date. Do not walk into the farm buildings unannounced.

faqs.q: Is the farm walk suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes, for children who can walk two to three hours with breaks. The path is mostly gentle going down, but the return is uphill. Carry water and snacks, and arrange a car for the way back if the children are young.

faqs.q: What crops will we see around Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: Maize, millet and paddy on the terraces, large cardamom in the shade of alder trees, ginger, seasonal vegetables and orange trees around houses. What you see depends on the month: maize stands tall in summer, oranges ripen from November to January.

faqs.q: Is Rinchenpong worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want quiet, a wide Kangchenjunga view and history rather than sightseeing lists. The 1730 monastery with its rare Ati Buddha, the Poison Lake story, Reesum Gumpa and farm walks fill two days well. Travellers who want shopping, nightlife or many hotels will be happier in Pelling, 31 km away.

faqs.q: How many days do we need in Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: Two nights is right for most travellers. That gives two chances at a clear sunrise, a morning for the monastery and Poison Lake, an afternoon for Reesum Gumpa or a farm walk, and time to sit and watch the range. One night is often lost to cloud.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest views of Kangchenjunga and comfortable days of 15–20 °C. February to April is also good, with flowering trees and some haze. January is cold but often clear. June to September brings heavy rain, leeches and cloud, though prices drop.

faqs.q: How far is Rinchenpong from Pelling?
faqs.a: About 31 km by road via Gyalshing and Legship, 1.5–2 hours by car. A reserved small car costs about ₹2,000–2,500 one way. Many travellers combine the two: two nights in Pelling for its sights and two in Rinchenpong for quiet and views.

faqs.q: How do I reach Rinchenpong from Siliguri or NJP?
faqs.a: By car it is about 115–125 km and 4.5–5 hours via Sevoke, Melli and Jorethang, costing about ₹4,500–6,000 for a small car. By shared jeep, go Siliguri–Jorethang, then Jorethang–Rinchenpong. NH10 along the Teesta closes after monsoon slides; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit to visit Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need a permit for Rinchenpong. Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, which since January 2026 is applied for online on the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India. Sikkim also charges a ₹50 tourist fee, collected by hotels. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs and shops in Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: There are small grocery shops and tea stalls but no ATM we would rely on. Carry enough cash for homestays, cars and meals. The nearest dependable ATMs are in Soreng, about 18 km away, and Jorethang, about 32 km. UPI works in some places when mobile data is available.

faqs.q: Is Rinchenpong good for a family holiday?
faqs.a: Yes, for families who enjoy walks and quiet. Distances are short, the altitude of about 1,650 m causes no breathing problems, and homestays cook simple food children eat. There are no amusement parks or malls. Pair it with Pelling for more sightseeing.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: Summer days reach about 20–25 °C and winter nights fall to 2–5 °C. From June to September expect heavy rain most days. October to March is dry and mostly clear, with cold mornings and evenings. The ridge is breezy, so a windproof jacket helps in any season.
